issues.legal_issue: A request to amend pleadings after trial has commenced is barred unless the party establishes that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier.
material_facts: The application to amend the written statement was filed after issues had been framed and the parties had submitted affidavits of evidence, with cross-examination dates fixed.
The trial court found that the matters sought to be added were within the applicants’ knowledge, or could have been known to them, before the written statement was filed.
The applicants did not establish that due diligence had prevented them from raising those matters before trial commenced.
issues.conclusion: The mandatory condition in the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 was not satisfied, so the amendment could not be allowed; the High Court’s order allowing it was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended by the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, 2002, bars amendment after commencement of trial unless the court concludes that, despite due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter earlier. The proviso restricts the court’s jurisdiction. The Court relied on Ajendraprasadji N. Pandey v. Swami Keshavprakeshdasji N. and Salem Advocate Bar Assn. v. Union of India, and distinguished Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh, where the parties had yet to file their documents.

predicates.civil_suit_pleading_amendment: A party in a civil suit applied to amend its pleadings.
predicates.trial_commenced: The suit had reached the stage at which trial had commenced.
predicates.party_failed_to_show_due_diligence_preve: The party did not establish that, despite due diligence, it could not have raised the proposed matter before trial commenced.

issues.definition: When a party in a civil suit seeks a pleading amendment after trial has commenced and fails to establish that due diligence prevented an earlier pleading, the amendment is barred.

issues.legal_issue: In a civil suit, trial commences when issues are framed and the case proceeds to the recording of evidence, including when evidence-in-chief is submitted by affidavit.
material_facts: Issues had been framed in the civil suit.
The parties had submitted affidavits of evidence, and dates had been fixed for cross-examination of the witnesses.
issues.conclusion: The trial had commenced before the application to amend the written statement was filed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Order XVIII Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, under which examination-in-chief is by affidavit, and read it with Order VI Rule 17. It relied on Union of India v. Major General Madan Lal Yadav for the principle that trial begins with the first necessary step in conducting it; Ameer Trading Corpn. Ltd. v. Shapoorji Data Processing Ltd. on affidavit evidence and the stages of witness examination; and Kailash v. Nanhku, which states that in a civil suit trial begins when issues are framed and the case is set down for evidence. The Court explained that Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh did not establish that trial cannot commence before the final hearing.

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding was a civil suit.
predicates.issues_framed: The court had framed the issues in the suit.
predicates.evidence_in_chief_submitted_by_affidavit: A party had submitted a witness’s evidence-in-chief by affidavit.

issues.definition: In a civil suit, when issues have been framed and evidence-in-chief has been submitted by affidavit, the trial has commenced.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court’s order allowing a pleading amendment cannot stand when it fails to address the jurisdictional issue and does not find that the trial court committed a jurisdictional or legal error.
material_facts: The High Court allowed the amendment despite the trial court’s refusal and without addressing the jurisdictional issue raised under the restriction on post-commencement amendments.
The High Court did not find that the trial court had exceeded its jurisdiction or committed an error of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s order could not be sustained and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the High Court’s judgment did not satisfy the test of judicial review because it did not address the contentions concerning the trial court’s jurisdiction and did not find that the trial court had exceeded its jurisdiction or committed an error of law.

predicates.review_of_trial_court_order: A reviewing court considered a challenge to a trial court’s order.
predicates.reviewing_court_ignored_jurisdictional_i: The reviewing court did not address the jurisdictional issue raised in the challenge.
predicates.no_finding_of_trial_court_jurisdictional: The reviewing court did not find that the trial court exceeded its jurisdiction or committed an error of law.

issues.definition: When a reviewing court ignores the jurisdictional issue and makes no finding that the trial court committed a jurisdictional or legal error, its order is unsustainable.
